A. Multiple Choice Questions

Q1. (c) its second focus

Official Answer

Q2. (b) a convexo-concave lens is thicker in the middle and has a converging action. A convexo-concave lens is thinner in the middle (not thicker), so it does not have a converging action.

Official Answer

Q3. (d) (2) only. A convex lens is thick in the middle (not thin), so statement (1) is wrong. A convex lens has a real focus and concave lens has a virtual focus, so statement (3) is wrong. Only statement (2) is correct.

Official Answer

Q4. (b) its first focus. A ray passing through the first focus (F₁) of a convex lens, or directed towards the first focus of a concave lens, emerges parallel to the principal axis after refraction.

Official Answer

Q5. (c) the radii of curvature of the two surfaces of the lens are equal.

Official Answer

Q6. (d) both (a) and (c). The focal length of a lens depends on the refractive index of the lens material relative to the surrounding medium, and on the radii of curvature of its two surfaces.

Official Answer

Q7. (a) increases. When a lens is placed in water, the difference in refractive index between the lens material and the surrounding medium decreases. This reduces the refracting power of the lens, so the focal length increases.

Official Answer

Q8. (d) does not change, decreases. Covering half the lens does not change its focal length (the remaining part still refracts light at the same focal point). However, less light enters the lens so the intensity of the image decreases.

Official Answer

Q9. (b) more. A thin convex lens has a longer focal length than a thick convex lens. A thicker lens bends light more strongly, converging rays at a nearer point (shorter focal length).

Official Answer

Q10. (c) f. When a lens is divided by a plane parallel to its principal axis, each half retains the same curvatures and the same optical centre distance. The focal length of each half remains f (the same as the original lens), though the image will be less bright.

Official Answer

Q11. (b) 10 cm. Using lens formula: 1/f = 1/v − 1/u = 1/20 − 1/(−20) = 1/20 + 1/20 = 2/20 = 1/10. Therefore f = 10 cm.

Official Answer

Q12. (c) virtual and enlarged. When the object is between O and F of a convex lens, the refracted rays diverge and when extended back, they meet on the same side as the object, forming a virtual, erect and magnified image.

Official Answer

Q13. (b) virtual, upright, and diminished. A concave (diverging) lens always forms an image that is virtual (cannot be formed on a screen), upright (same orientation as the object), and diminished (smaller than the object), regardless of the object's position.

Official Answer

Q14. (b) 2F₂. When an object is placed at 2F₁ (i.e., at a distance of 2f from the lens), the image is formed at 2F₂ on the other side of the lens. The image is real, inverted and of the same size as the object.

Official Answer

Q15. (d) in Galilean telescope. A concave (diverging) lens is used as the eyepiece in a Galilean telescope. The other options (slide projector, magnifying glass, burning glass) all use convex (converging) lenses.

Official Answer

Q16. (a) 1/v − 1/u = 1/f. According to the new Cartesian sign convention, the lens formula is 1/v − 1/u = 1/f, where u is the object distance, v is the image distance, and f is the focal length. All distances are measured from the optical centre of the lens.

Official Answer

Q17. (d) the image is real and diminished. A negative magnification indicates the image is real and inverted. A magnitude of 0.5 (less than 1) indicates the image is diminished. This corresponds to a convex lens with the object beyond 2F.

Official Answer

Q18. (b) increases. Power P = 1/f (in metres). As focal length decreases, power increases (they are inversely related). A lens with shorter focal length bends light more strongly and thus has greater power.

Official Answer

Q19. (b) convex of focal length 1.0 m. P = 1/f → f = 1/P = 1/1.0 = 1.0 m. The positive sign indicates it is a convex (converging) lens.

Official Answer

Q20. (b) 25 cm. The least distance of distinct vision (also called the near point) of a normal human eye is 25 cm. Objects closer than this cannot be seen clearly without optical aid.

Official Answer

Q21. (c) a virtual and magnified image. A magnifying glass is a convex lens used with the object placed between the optical centre and the focus. This produces a virtual, erect and magnified image on the same side as the object.

Official Answer

Q22. (c) virtual, diminished. A concave (diverging) lens always produces a virtual, erect and diminished image, regardless of the position of the object in front of it.

Official Answer

Q23. (a) m < 1 (between 0 and 1). A concave lens always forms a diminished, virtual, erect image. Since the image is smaller than the object, magnification is always between 0 and 1 (i.e., 0 < m < 1) and always positive (erect image).

Official Answer

Q24. (d) virtual and magnified. A positive magnification indicates the image is virtual and erect. A magnitude of 2 (greater than 1) indicates the image is magnified. This corresponds to a convex lens used as a magnifying glass (object between O and F).

Official Answer

Q25. (b) away from the lens. Using lens formula: u = −20 cm, f = +12 cm. 1/v = 1/f + 1/u = 1/12 − 1/20 = 5/60 − 3/60 = 2/60 = 1/30. Therefore v = 30 cm. The clear image forms at 30 cm from the lens, but the screen is at 23 cm. The screen must be moved away from the lens (by 7 cm).

Official Answer

B. Very Short Answer Questions

Q26. A lens is a piece of transparent refracting material bounded by two curved surfaces (usually spherical), or one curved and one plane surface. A lens refracts light passing through it. Lenses are broadly classified into two types: convex (converging) lenses and concave (diverging) lenses.

Model Answer (not an official mark scheme)

Q27. (i) An equiconvex lens is converging. It is thicker at the middle and thinner at the edges, causing parallel rays to converge.
(ii) A concavo-convex lens is converging. In a concavo-convex lens, the convex surface has a smaller radius of curvature than the concave surface, so the lens is thicker in the middle and acts as a converging lens.

Official Answer

Q28. A lens is called equiconvex or equiconcave when the radii of curvature of its two surfaces are equal.

Official Answer

Q29. The focal length of a lens is the distance between the optical centre of the lens and its principal focus (second focus). It is denoted by f. For a convex lens, f is positive; for a concave lens, f is negative.

Model Answer (not an official mark scheme)

Q30. The focal plane of a lens is the plane perpendicular to the principal axis of the lens, passing through the principal focus. Parallel oblique rays (not parallel to the principal axis) converge at a point on the focal plane after refraction through a convex lens.

Model Answer (not an official mark scheme)

Q31. (a) does not change; decreases. Covering half the lens does not alter the focal length, but less light passes through so the image is less bright (lower intensity).
(b) more (greater). A thinner lens has a longer focal length because it bends light less strongly.
(c) biconvex. A water-filled tumbler is thicker at the centre and forms a converging lens.

Official Answer

Q32. (a) Convex (converging) lens.
(b) The image is real. A convex lens forms an inverted image only when the object is placed beyond the focus. Such an image is always real.

Official Answer

Q33. (a) Concave (diverging) lens.
(b) The image is always diminished (smaller than the object). A concave lens always forms a virtual, erect and diminished image regardless of the position of the object.

Official Answer

Q34. No. A concave lens cannot form an image of size two times the object. A concave lens diverges the rays incident on it, and the image formed is always diminished (magnification is always between 0 and 1). It can never form a magnified image.

Official Answer

Q35. The image formed by a concave lens is always:
1. Virtual (cannot be obtained on a screen)
2. Diminished (smaller than the object)
It is also always erect (upright) and forms on the same side as the object.

Official Answer

Q36. When a convex lens forms a virtual image (object between O and F), the image is:
1. Erect (upright) — in the same orientation as the object
2. Magnified (larger than the object)

Official Answer

Q37. (i) Positive focal length → Convex (converging) lens. A convex lens causes incident parallel rays to converge at the principal focus on the other side of the lens, so its focal length is taken as positive.
(ii) Negative focal length → Concave (diverging) lens. A concave lens causes incident parallel rays to diverge, appearing to come from a virtual focus on the same side as the incident light, so its focal length is taken as negative.

Official Answer

Q38. From the sign of magnification (m):
(i) + sign → the image is virtual (and erect). The image forms on the same side as the object.
− sign → the image is real (and inverted). The image forms on the opposite side from the object.
(ii) + sign → the image is erect (upright).
− sign → the image is inverted.

Official Answer

Q39. Power gets halved. Since P = 1/f (in metres), when f is doubled, P becomes 1/(2f) = P/2. So the power is halved.

Official Answer

Q40. + sign → convergent action (convex lens). The lens converges the incident rays towards its centre.
− sign → divergent action (concave lens). The lens diverges the incident rays away from its centre.

Official Answer

Q41. A magnifying glass (simple microscope) is a convex lens of short focal length used to view small objects placed between its optical centre and its principal focus, producing a virtual, erect and magnified image.
Two uses:
1. Used by jewellers, watchmakers, and stamp collectors to see minute details of objects.
2. Used as a reading glass to read small print in books, maps and newspapers.

Model Answer (not an official mark scheme)

Q42. Concave (diverging) lens. A concave lens always forms a virtual, erect and diminished image for any position of the object.

Official Answer

Q43. (i) When a lens is placed in water, its focal length increases. This is because the difference between the refractive index of the lens material and the surrounding medium (water) is less than that between the lens and air. Reduced refractive contrast means weaker bending of light, hence a longer focal length.
(ii) A thin lens has a greater focal length than a thick lens. A thicker lens has a more curved surface and bends light more strongly, giving a shorter focal length.

Official Answer

C. Short Answer Questions

Q44. The two kinds of lenses are:
1. Convex lens (converging lens): Thicker at the middle and thinner at the edges. It converges a parallel beam of light rays to a point on the other side.
2. Concave lens (diverging lens): Thinner at the middle and thicker at the edges. It diverges a parallel beam of light rays.
Convex lenses include biconvex, plano-convex, and convexo-concave. Concave lenses include biconcave, plano-concave, and concavo-convex.

Model Answer (not an official mark scheme)

Q45. (a) Appearance:
• Convex lens: Thicker at the centre (middle) and thinner at the edges.
• Concave lens: Thinner at the centre (middle) and thicker at the edges.

(b) Action on incident light:
• Convex lens: Converges (brings together) a parallel beam of incident rays towards the principal axis after refraction. It has a real principal focus.
• Concave lens: Diverges (spreads apart) a parallel beam of incident rays away from the principal axis after refraction. It has a virtual principal focus.

Model Answer (not an official mark scheme)

Q46. The optical centre (O) of a lens is a point on the principal axis of the lens through which a ray of light passes without any deviation (without bending). For a ray passing through the optical centre, the incident and emergent rays are parallel, though slightly displaced. In a double convex or double concave lens, the optical centre lies at the geometric centre of the lens on the principal axis.

Model Answer (not an official mark scheme)

Q47. The three principal (standard) rays used to construct a ray diagram for a lens are:

1. Ray parallel to the principal axis: After refraction through a convex lens, it passes through the second principal focus F₂. For a concave lens, it appears to diverge from the second focus F₂.

2. Ray passing through the optical centre O: This ray passes undeviated (without bending) through the lens for both convex and concave lenses.

3. Ray passing through (or directed towards) the first principal focus F₁: After refraction through a convex lens, it emerges parallel to the principal axis. For a concave lens, a ray directed towards F₁ emerges parallel to the principal axis.

The intersection of any two of the refracted rays gives the position of the image.

Model Answer (not an official mark scheme)

Q48. Real image:
1. Formed by actual intersection of refracted (or reflected) rays.
2. Can be obtained on a screen.
3. Is always inverted with respect to the object.
4. Is formed on the opposite side of the lens from the object (for a convex lens).

Virtual image:
1. Formed by the apparent (imaginary) intersection of rays when produced backwards.
2. Cannot be obtained on a screen.
3. Is always erect with respect to the object.
4. Is formed on the same side as the object (for a lens).

Model Answer (not an official mark scheme)

Q49. (a) At infinity: The object must be placed at the principal focus F₁ (at a distance equal to the focal length f in front of the lens).
(b) Same size as the object: The object must be placed at 2F₁ (at a distance equal to 2f from the lens). The image forms at 2F₂ — real, inverted and same size.
(c) Inverted and enlarged: The object must be placed between F₁ and 2F₁ (between f and 2f from the lens). The image forms beyond 2F₂ — real, inverted and magnified.
(d) Upright and enlarged: The object must be placed between the optical centre O and the focus F₁ (at a distance less than f). The image is virtual, erect and magnified, on the same side as the object.

Official Answer

Q50. | Type of lens | Position of object | Nature of image | Size of image |
|--------------|--------------------|-----------------|---------------|
| Convex | Between O and F | Virtual, erect | Magnified |
| Convex | At focus F₁ | Real, inverted (at infinity) | Infinitely large |
| Concave | At infinity | Virtual, erect | Highly diminished (point-sized) |
| Concave | At any distance | Virtual, erect | Diminished |

Model Answer (not an official mark scheme)

Q51. New Cartesian Sign Convention for lenses:
1. All distances are measured from the optical centre (O) of the lens.
2. Distances measured in the direction of the incident light (i.e., on the side of the transmitted/refracted light) are taken as positive.
3. Distances measured against the direction of the incident light (i.e., on the side of the object) are taken as negative.
4. The object is always placed to the left of the lens, so the object distance (u) is always negative.
5. For a convex lens, the focal length (f) is positive; for a concave lens, f is negative.
6. Heights measured above the principal axis are positive; heights below are negative.

Model Answer (not an official mark scheme)

Q52. Lens formula: 1/v − 1/u = 1/f

Where:
• v = image distance, measured from the optical centre to the image (positive if on the same side as the transmitted light, negative if on the same side as the object)
• u = object distance, measured from the optical centre to the object (always negative, as the object is always on the side of incident light)
• f = focal length of the lens (positive for convex lens, negative for concave lens)

Model Answer (not an official mark scheme)

Q53. Magnification (m) produced by a lens is defined as the ratio of the height of the image to the height of the object. It tells us how many times the image is larger (or smaller) than the object.

Expression: m = I/O = v/u

Where:
• m = magnification (dimensionless)
• I = height of the image (positive if erect, negative if inverted)
• O = height of the object (always positive)
• v = image distance (from optical centre)
• u = object distance (from optical centre)

If m > 1: image is magnified; if m < 1: image is diminished; if m = 1: image is same size.
If m is positive: image is virtual and erect; if m is negative: image is real and inverted.

Model Answer (not an official mark scheme)

Q54. Power of a lens is defined as the reciprocal of its focal length expressed in metres.

P = 1/f (where f is in metres)

Power measures the degree to which a lens converges or diverges light. A lens with shorter focal length has greater power.

Unit: Dioptre (D). One dioptre is the power of a lens of focal length 1 metre.

Convex (converging) lens: positive power.
Concave (diverging) lens: negative power.

Model Answer (not an official mark scheme)

Q55. Applications of a convex lens:
1. Used as a magnifying glass (simple microscope) to view small objects.
2. Used in cameras, projectors, slide projectors, and cinema projectors to form real images.
3. Used in spectacles to correct long-sightedness (hypermetropia).
(Any two of the above)

Applications of a concave lens:
1. Used in spectacles to correct short-sightedness (myopia).
2. Used as the eyepiece in Galilean telescopes and in some binoculars.
3. Used as a spy hole (peephole) in doors to give a wide field of view.
(Any two of the above)

Model Answer (not an official mark scheme)

Q56. (i) For a real, same-size image: The object must be placed at 2F₁ (at a distance equal to twice the focal length, i.e., at 2f from the lens). The image forms at 2F₂ — real, inverted and the same size as the object.

(ii) For use as a magnifying lens: The object must be placed between the optical centre O and the principal focus F₁ (at a distance less than the focal length f). This produces a virtual, erect and magnified image on the same side as the object.

Official Answer

Q57. (a) In a reading glass, the object (printed page) is placed between the optical centre (O) and the principal focus (F₁) of the convex lens, i.e., at a distance less than the focal length from the lens. This produces a virtual, erect and magnified image.

(b) A concave lens cannot be used as a reading glass (magnifying glass) because it always forms a virtual, erect and diminished image, regardless of the position of the object. It reduces the apparent size of the object rather than magnifying it.

Official Answer

Q58. The lens is a concave (diverging) lens. A concave lens always produces a virtual, erect and diminished image for any position of the object.

One use: Used in spectacles to correct short-sightedness (myopia). A concave lens diverges light rays so that they appear to come from the far point of the myopic eye, allowing the person to see distant objects clearly.

Official Answer

Q59. (i) Enlarged real image: The object must be placed between F₁ and 2F₁ (between f and 2f from the lens). The image forms beyond 2F₂ — real, inverted and magnified.

(ii) Enlarged virtual image: The object must be placed between the optical centre O and the focus F₁ (at a distance less than f). The image forms on the same side as the object — virtual, erect and magnified (this is the magnifying glass arrangement).

Official Answer

D. Long Answer Questions

Q60. (a) The object is placed between F₁ and 2F₁ (i.e., between f and 2f in front of the lens).

(b) Ray diagram: Draw two rays from the top of the object — one parallel to the principal axis that passes through F₂ after refraction, and one directed towards the optical centre that passes undeviated. The intersection of refracted rays beyond 2F₂ gives the image position.

(c) Three characteristics of the image:
1. Real — the image is formed by actual intersection of refracted rays and can be obtained on a screen.
2. Inverted — the image is upside down relative to the object.
3. Magnified — the image is larger than the object.

Q61. (a) The object is placed at 2F₁ (at a distance equal to twice the focal length of the lens).

(b) Ray diagram: Object AB placed at 2F₁. Ray from A parallel to axis refracts through F₂. Ray from A through optical centre passes undeviated. Both refracted rays meet at A' at 2F₂, forming image A'B' at 2F₂.

(c) Two more characteristics of the image:
1. Real — formed by actual intersection of refracted rays; can be obtained on a screen.
2. Inverted — the image is upside down relative to the object.

Q62. (a) Convex (converging) lens.

(b) The object is placed between the optical centre O and the principal focus F₁ (at a distance less than the focal length f from the lens).

(c) Ray diagram: Object AB placed between O and F₁. Ray from A parallel to principal axis refracts and passes through F₂ (or its extension). Ray from A through O passes undeviated. The two refracted rays diverge; when extended back, they appear to come from A'. The virtual image A'B' is formed on the same side as the object, beyond the object (farther from the lens).

(d) The device is a simple microscope (magnifying glass or reading glass).

Model Answer (not an official mark scheme)

Q63. (a) Concave (diverging) lens.

(b) Ray diagram: Object AB placed at any distance in front of a concave lens. Ray from A parallel to the principal axis refracts and appears to diverge from F₂ (on the same side as the object). Ray from A directed towards the optical centre O passes undeviated. The two refracted rays diverge; when extended back, they appear to meet at A' between the object and the lens. The image A'B' is formed between the object and the lens.

(c) Three characteristics of the image:
1. Virtual — formed by the apparent intersection of diverging rays; cannot be obtained on a screen.
2. Erect — the image is upright, same orientation as the object.
3. Diminished — the image is smaller than the object.

Q64. A magnifying glass is a convex lens of short focal length. The object is placed between the optical centre O and the principal focus F₁ of the lens.

Ray diagram: Object AB placed between O and F₁ (closer to the lens than the focal length).
• Ray 1: From tip A, parallel to the principal axis → after refraction, it appears to come from F₂ (on the same side as the object).
• Ray 2: From tip A, through the optical centre O → passes undeviated.
• The two refracted rays diverge on the other side. When extended back, they meet at A', which is farther from the lens on the same side as the object.
• The image A'B' is formed on the same side as the object, behind the object (farther from the lens).
• The eye is placed close to the lens on the opposite side to observe the virtual image.

Three characteristics of the image:
1. Virtual — cannot be obtained on a screen.
2. Erect — upright, same orientation as the object.
3. Magnified — larger than the object.

Model Answer (not an official mark scheme)

Q65. As the object is moved from infinity towards the convex lens:

1. Object at infinity:
Position of image: At F₂ (second focus)
Size: Highly diminished (point-sized)
Nature: Real, inverted

2. Object beyond 2F₁:
Position: Between F₂ and 2F₂
Size: Diminished
Nature: Real, inverted

3. Object at 2F₁:
Position: At 2F₂
Size: Same size as object
Nature: Real, inverted

4. Object between F₁ and 2F₁:
Position: Beyond 2F₂
Size: Magnified
Nature: Real, inverted

5. Object at F₁:
Position: At infinity
Size: Infinitely large
Nature: Real, inverted

6. Object between F₁ and O:
Position: On same side as object (beyond object)
Size: Magnified
Nature: Virtual, erect

Summary: As the object moves from infinity to the lens, the image moves from F₂ towards infinity (real, inverted), then reappears on the same side as the object and moves from infinity towards the object (virtual, erect, magnified).

Model Answer (not an official mark scheme)

Q66. For a concave lens, regardless of where the object is placed, the image is always virtual, erect and diminished. However, the position and size of the image change as follows:

1. Object at infinity:
Position: At F₂ (on the same side as the object, at the focus of the concave lens)
Size: Highly diminished (point-sized)
Nature: Virtual, erect

2. Object at any finite distance (e.g., beyond 2F, at 2F, between F and 2F, at F):
Position: Between O and F₂ (on the same side as the object, between the optical centre and the focus)
Size: Diminished (gets larger as the object moves closer)
Nature: Virtual, erect

3. As the object moves from infinity towards the lens:
- The image moves from F₂ towards the optical centre O.
- The image remains virtual, erect and diminished throughout.
- The image size increases as the object gets closer.

4. When the object is at the lens (u → 0):
The image coincides with the object.

Model Answer (not an official mark scheme)

Q67. A diverging (concave) lens spreads out (diverges) the rays of light that fall on it. No matter where the object is placed in front of a concave lens, the refracted rays always diverge on the other side of the lens. These diverging rays, when extended backwards, appear to meet on the same side as the object.

Since the refracted rays diverge and never actually meet on the other side of the lens, they cannot form a real image (real images require actual intersection of refracted rays). All images formed by a concave lens are virtual (formed by the apparent/imaginary intersection of rays).

Ray diagram explanation: Object AB placed in front of concave lens.
• Ray from A parallel to axis → after refraction, diverges appearing to come from F₂.
• Ray from A through O → passes undeviated.
• Both refracted rays diverge — they do not actually intersect anywhere on the right side of the lens.
• Extending the diverging rays back to the left, they appear to meet at A' on the same side as the object — a virtual image.

Model Answer (not an official mark scheme)

Q68. When an object AB is placed between O and F₁ of a converging lens:

Three standard rays from point A:
1. Ray parallel to the principal axis → after refraction, passes through F₂.
2. Ray through optical centre O → passes undeviated.
3. Ray directed towards F₁ → after refraction, emerges parallel to the principal axis.

The three refracted rays all diverge on the right side. When extended backwards, they appear to meet at A' on the left side (same side as the object), forming the virtual image A'B'.

Three characteristics of the image:
1. Virtual — formed by the apparent intersection of rays; cannot be obtained on a screen.
2. Erect — upright, same orientation as the object.
3. Magnified — larger than the object.

Device: Simple microscope (magnifying glass / reading glass).

Model Answer (not an official mark scheme)

Q69. A convex lens has two principal foci:

First Principal Focus (F₁): The first principal focus F₁ is a point on the principal axis of the convex lens such that rays of light starting from this point (or directed towards it) become parallel to the principal axis after refraction through the lens. F₁ is on the same side as the incident light (in front of the lens).

Second Principal Focus (F₂): The second principal focus F₂ is a point on the principal axis such that rays of light incident parallel to the principal axis, after refraction through the lens, converge at this point. F₂ is on the other side of the lens (behind the lens, on the side of the transmitted light).

For a convex lens, both F₁ and F₂ are real. F₂ is the more commonly used focus for image formation by a camera, projector, etc.

Model Answer (not an official mark scheme)

Q70. A concave lens has two principal foci:

First Principal Focus (F₁): The first principal focus F₁ is a point on the principal axis of the concave lens such that rays of light directed towards this point, after refraction through the lens, become parallel to the principal axis. F₁ is on the other side of the lens from the incident light (behind the lens).

Second Principal Focus (F₂): The second principal focus F₂ is a point on the principal axis such that rays of light incident parallel to the principal axis, after refraction through the lens, appear to diverge from this point. F₂ is on the same side as the incident light (in front of the lens, on the side of the object).

For a concave lens, both F₁ and F₂ are virtual (no actual rays pass through them).

Model Answer (not an official mark scheme)

Q71. (a) Ray diagram: Object AB placed at 2F₁.
• Ray from A parallel to axis → refracts through F₂.
• Ray from A through O → passes undeviated.
• The two refracted rays meet at A' at 2F₂.
• Image A'B' is formed at 2F₂ — real, inverted, same size as object.

(b) Change in image size with a lens of greater focal length:
If the focal length f is increased (with the object remaining at the same position), the object is now placed closer to the lens than 2F (i.e., the object is between F and 2F of the new lens). According to the image formation rules for a convex lens:
- Object between F and 2F → image beyond 2F on the other side.
- The image becomes larger (magnified) compared to the original same-size image.
Therefore, the size of the image increases (becomes magnified) when the lens is replaced with one of greater focal length.

Official Answer

E. Numericals

Q72. Given: O = 3 cm, I = 6 cm (inverted, so negative in sign convention, but magnitude used for size), v = +30 cm.

(a) Finding object distance (u):
m = I/O = v/u
Magnification m = −I/O = −6/3 = −2 (negative because real, inverted)
∴ m = v/u → −2 = 30/u → u = 30/(−2) = −15 cm

The candle must be placed 15 cm in front of the lens.

(b) Finding focal length (f):
1/f = 1/v − 1/u = 1/30 − 1/(−15) = 1/30 + 1/15 = 1/30 + 2/30 = 3/30 = 1/10
f = 10 cm

The focal length of the convex lens is 10 cm.

Official Answer

Q73. (a) Nature of the image: The image is virtual, erect and diminished. It is on the same side as the object (as stated in the problem).

(b) Given: u = −20 cm (object in front of lens), v = −10 cm (image on same side as object, hence negative)

Using lens formula: 1/f = 1/v − 1/u = 1/(−10) − 1/(−20) = −1/10 + 1/20 = −2/20 + 1/20 = −1/20

∴ f = −20 cm

The focal length of the concave lens is 20 cm (negative, confirming it is a concave lens).

Q74. Given: f = +25 cm (convex lens), m = +2 (virtual image, erect, magnified)

For a virtual image formed by a convex lens:
m = v/u
+2 = v/u → v = 2u

Since both image and object are on the same side (virtual image): u = −u₀ (negative), v = −v₀ (negative for virtual image in convex lens)
m = v/u = (−v₀)/(−u₀) = v₀/u₀ = 2 → v₀ = 2u₀, so v = 2u (both negative)

Using lens formula: 1/f = 1/v − 1/u = 1/(2u) − 1/u = 1/(2u) − 2/(2u) = −1/(2u)
25 = −2u → but u is negative, so u = −12.5 cm

Verification: u = −12.5 cm, v = 2u = −25 cm
1/f = 1/(−25) − 1/(−12.5) = −1/25 + 2/25 = 1/25 ✓ → f = 25 cm ✓

The object must be placed 12.5 cm in front of the lens (between O and F).

Official Answer

Q75. Given: f = +0.12 m = 12 cm (convex lens), m = −3 (real image, inverted, 3 times magnified)

m = v/u → −3 = v/u → v = −3u

Since u is negative (object in front of lens): let u = −d, then v = −3(−d) = 3d (positive, on other side)

Using lens formula: 1/f = 1/v − 1/u
1/12 = 1/(3d) − 1/(−d) = 1/(3d) + 1/d = 1/(3d) + 3/(3d) = 4/(3d)
3d = 4 × 12 = 48 → d = 16 cm

So u = −16 cm = −0.16 m, and v = 3 × 16 = 48 cm = 0.48 m

The object must be placed 0.16 m (16 cm) in front of the lens. The image forms at 0.48 m (48 cm) behind the lens.

Official Answer

Q76. Given: v = +75 cm, total distance = 100 cm, so u = −(100 − 75) = −25 cm

1/f = 1/v − 1/u = 1/75 − 1/(−25) = 1/75 + 1/25 = 1/75 + 3/75 = 4/75
f = 75/4 = 18.75 cm

The focal length of the lens = 18.75 cm

(ii) Magnification:
m = v/u = 75/(−25) = −3

The magnification = −3 (negative sign indicates real, inverted image that is 3 times the size of the object).

Q77. Given: u = −15 cm (object in front), image is 60 cm in front of lens → v = −60 cm (same side as object, so virtual image)

1/f = 1/v − 1/u = 1/(−60) − 1/(−15) = −1/60 + 1/15 = −1/60 + 4/60 = 3/60 = 1/20
f = +20 cm (positive → convex lens)

(ii) Magnification:
m = v/u = (−60)/(−15) = +4

(iii) Nature of image:
Since m = +4 (positive) → erect and virtual; magnitude 4 → magnified.
The image is virtual, erect and magnified (4 times the size of the object).

f = 30 cm

m = v/u = 90/(−45) = −2

Q92. Given: u = −45 cm (object in front of concave lens), v = −30 cm (image on same side as object, concave lens always forms virtual image)

Using lens formula:
1/f = 1/v − 1/u = 1/(−30) − 1/(−45) = −1/30 + 1/45

Finding common denominator (LCM of 30 and 45 = 90):
= −3/90 + 2/90 = −1/90

f = −90 cm

The focal length of the concave lens is 90 cm (negative confirming it is concave).

Q93. Step 1: When image is same size as object, the object is at 2F (distance = 2f from lens).
So initial object distance u₁ = −2f, image distance v₁ = +2f

Step 2: Object moved 12 cm closer → new object distance u₂ = −(2f − 12)
New magnification m₂ = −3 (real, inverted, 3× magnified)

m₂ = v₂/u₂ → −3 = v₂/[−(2f − 12)] → v₂ = 3(2f − 12)

Step 3: Apply lens formula for the new position:
1/f = 1/v₂ − 1/u₂ = 1/[3(2f−12)] − 1/[−(2f−12)]
= 1/[3(2f−12)] + 1/(2f−12)
= [1 + 3]/[3(2f−12)]
= 4/[3(2f−12)]

Therefore: f × 4 = 3(2f − 12)
4f = 6f − 36
36 = 2f
f = 18 cm

The focal length of the convex lens = 18 cm.

Q96. Given: P₁ = +2.5 D, P₂ = −2.5 D

Power of combination:
P = P₁ + P₂ = +2.5 + (−2.5) = 0 D

A combination of power 0 D has infinite focal length (f = 1/P → 1/0 = ∞).

The combination will behave like a glass plate (or plane glass) — it will neither converge nor diverge light. The parallel rays will pass through it without any deviation (as if no lens were present).
